system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-02-17 18:14:00 to 2174-02-19 16:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a one-week history of dry heaving and epigastric pain, recurring shortly after a prior hospitalization for similar symptoms. She has a complex surgical history including Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube placement due to prior GJ anastomotic ulcer. On admission, she was started on IV fluids, which resolved her symptoms. She remained hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and without leukocytosis. Laboratory results were largely normal, and she tolerated enteral nutrition via G-tube at full strength. Treatment included continuation of lansoprazole and rifaximin, with addition of sucralfate for gastric protection. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue medications and follow up with her specialist.
problems: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
Personal history of peptic ulcer disease

diagnoses.long_title: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting again. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same as last week. Any time I try to eat or drink, I feel sick and start vomiting. The pain is right here in my upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just here a week ago for similar symptoms. Since you have a G-tube, are you still able to take your feeds through it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube feeds are going okay. I haven’t had any issues with those. But anything by mouth makes me feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of gastric bypass and the GJ ulcer before, this could be gastritis. We’ll start you on IV fluids to rehydrate you and give you some anti-nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. Do you think it’s another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know for sure yet. Your CT scan from earlier didn’t show a blockage, which is reassuring. But we may need an endoscopy soon to look more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the last time I had that, they found the ulcer near the connection. Will they do that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the GI team will likely schedule an outpatient endoscopy next week. For now, we’ll focus on getting your symptoms under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ve also been worried because my belly wound has some drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that too. There’s some serous fluid at the base, and the wound is slightly open. We’ll keep it packed and clean. It doesn’t look infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I was worried about that. And my meds—I’m still on lansoprazole and rifaximin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re continuing both. We’re also adding sucralfate four times a day. It coats the stomach and helps protect the lining while it heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helps with ulcers, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s especially useful for people with your surgical history. We’ll give it to you through your G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. And for pain, can I still use the hydrocodone if it gets bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have hydro*mor*phone—Dilaudid—available every three hours as needed. But we’ll try to keep it minimal. The lansoprazole and sucralfate should help reduce irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll only use it if I really need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re also on ondansetron for nausea, which we’ll give every 12 hours as needed. Let the nurse know if you’re still feeling sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you for a couple of days to make sure you’re stable. If your symptoms improve and labs stay normal, you could go home by Thursday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. I haven’t vomited since yesterday evening, and the pain is less intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your labs from last night were normal—white count, kidney function, everything looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably just inflammation, not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no signs of infection. Your symptoms are most consistent with gastritis—stomach lining irritation—likely related to your surgical anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the reflux? I used to have that all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your reflux is listed in your history, and while it’s improved, it can still contribute. That’s why we keep you on high-dose lansoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my mental health meds—are they still being given?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluoxetine and aripiprazole are being given daily through your G-tube. Lorazepam for anxiety is also continued three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been feeling anxious about being back in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’re here to support you. The good news is you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’ve reviewed everything, and you’re doing well. The GI team saw you yesterday and will set up your endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discharge you this afternoon. Your symptoms have improved, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the sucralfate? Do I keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, four times a day for now. It helps protect your stomach while we figure out the exact cause with the endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to follow up with the weight loss surgery clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and GI will contact you to schedule the endoscopy. Keep using your G-tube for meds and feeds, and avoid eating by mouth for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready, and you should be home by early afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any new pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling much better. Wound is a little sore, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send instructions for wound care home with you. Keep it clean and monitor for redness or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And I’ll call if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also reach out if you have fever, severe pain, or can’t keep your feeds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll stay in touch with the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You’ll get a call from GI soon to schedule the endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your discharge paperwork. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep taking all your medications as prescribed, especially the sucralfate before meals and at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set reminders. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re feeling stable and ready for discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re discharged. Take care and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for recurrent epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting shortly after a prior hospitalization for similar symptoms. She has a complex history including Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube placement due to a previous GJ anastomotic ulcer. She remained on G-tube feeds throughout and was treated with IV fluids, anti-emetics, and continued proton-pump inhibition with lansoprazole. Sucralfate was added for gastric protection. Her symptoms improved over two days, and labs remained normal. The GI team evaluated her and will arrange an outpatient endoscopy to further investigate the cause of her abdominal pain. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue medications, avoid oral intake, and follow up with both the weight loss surgery clinic and GI.
problems: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
